title: Yaji with Onion and Garlic
author: Ronke Adeyemi
desc: Equal volumes of kuli kuli and ginger powder, with onion, garlic and paprika — combine thoroughly and that is the entire method.
longDesc: This is yaji at its simplest to make and its most different in composition: half a cup each of ground kuli kuli and ginger powder, a quarter cup each of chilli, paprika, onion powder and garlic powder, and a tablespoon of sea salt. No grinding, no sieving, no toasting — combine all the ingredients thoroughly and store in an airtight container. The ratio of kuli kuli to ginger is one to one by volume, which is a markedly gingerier blend than the weighed version, and the onion, garlic and paprika appear in no other documented yaji.
ingredients: 1/2 cup ground kuli kuli — or roasted groundnut powder as a substitute
steps: Combine all of the ingredients thoroughly in a bowl.
Store in an airtight container for future use.
chefTips: Kuli kuli over roasted groundnut powder, and the reason is stated: the lower oil content is what the author calls the secret to professional-quality suya spice. Peanut powder will clump.
One to one by volume, kuli kuli to ginger. That is far gingerier than the weighed blend at NGA079, where it is 110 g to 75 g. Taste both and pick.
The onion, garlic and paprika are unique to this blend. They make it rounder and less sharp, and more immediately recognisable to a palate used to barbecue rubs.
No sieving needed because there is no fibrous African negro pepper in it. That also means it is missing a flavour the other blends have.
Paprika contributes colour rather than heat. If your suya looks pale, this is the blend that fixes it.
An airtight container is specified rather than the freezer. Ginger powder keeps better cold, so the freezer is still worth it.
No cloves here either. The academic description of yaji treats clove as canonical and three of the four blog blends omit it — see NGA079.
commonMistakes: Substituting peanut powder and getting a paste.
Assuming this blend is interchangeable with the weighed one.
Leaving it in a warm cupboard for months.
Adding salt again when seasoning the meat.
Expecting the fibrous depth that negro pepper gives the other blends.
sources: Adapted from 'Nigerian Suya Spice Mix recipe (Yaji)', byline Ronke Edoho, 9jafoodie. Quantities exactly as printed: 1/2 cup grounded Kuli Kuli (Substitute roasted groundnut powder); 1/2 cup Ginger Powder; 1/4 cup Chilli Powder; 1/4 cup Paprika Powder; 1/4 cup Onion Powder; 1/4 cup Garlic Powder; 1 table spoon sea salt. Yield not given.
The method is the entire method, verbatim: 'Combine all of the ingredients thoroughly' and 'Store in an air tight container for future use.'

HEADNOTE, and it is the clearest statement anywhere of why kuli kuli is the correct ingredient: the author explains that kuli kuli is superior to a fresh peanut blend because of its lower oil content, and calls this 'the secret' to professional-quality suya spice.
KULI KULI TO GINGER IS 1:1 BY VOLUME here. Contrast NGA079's 110 g to 75 g and NGA081's 100 g to 2 tablespoons. Three named sources, three substantially different ratios, not averaged.

UNIQUE TO THIS BLEND: paprika, onion powder and garlic powder, which appear in no other documented yaji. It also has no stock cube and no African negro pepper, both of which the weighed blend includes.

NO CLOVES, as with two of the other three blog blends. The academic description of yaji — Erhirhie Earnest Oghenesuvwe, Trends in Applied Sciences Research, 2019 — establishes clove and black pepper as canonical constituents while giving no quantities at all. Ginger is the only ingredient all the documented blends share.
storage: 6 months in an airtight container, longer in the freezer.
healthBenefits: Defatted groundnut cake is high in protein and low in fat.
Garlic and onion powder carry organosulfur compounds.
culturalNote: The difference between this blend and the weighed one is a good illustration of how a trade spice becomes a home spice. Onion powder, garlic powder and paprika are pantry items rather than northern market items, and their presence here marks a blend assembled by a cook working from what is available rather than from what a Mai Suya would reach for.
